title: Batch Normalization: Accelerating Deep Network Training by Reducing Internal Covariate Shift (Ioffe & Szegedy, 2015)
excerpt: Consider a mini-batch B of size m. Since the normalization is applied to each activation independently, let us focus on a particular activation x and omit k for clarity. We have m values of this activation in the mini-batch, B = {x_1...m}. Let the normalized values be x̂_1...m, and their linear transformations be y_1...m. We refer to the transform BN_γ,β : x_1...m → y_1...m as the Batch Normalizing Transform. Algorithm 1: Input: Values of x over a mini-batch: B = {x_1...m}; Parameters to be learned: γ, β. Output: {y_i = BN_γ,β(x_i)}. μ_B ← (1/m) Σ_{i=1}^m x_i // mini-batch mean. σ²_B ← (1/m) Σ_{i=1}^m (x_i − μ_B)² // mini-batch variance. x̂_i ← (x_i − μ_B) / sqrt(σ²_B + ε) // normalize. y_i ← γ x̂_i + β ≡ BN_γ,β(x_i) // scale and shift. In the algorithm, ε is a constant added to the mini-batch variance for numerical stability. Note that simply normalizing each input of a layer may change what the layer can represent. To address this, we make sure that the transformation inserted in the network can represent the identity transform: by setting γ = sqrt(Var[x]) and β = E[x], we could recover the original activations, if that were the optimal thing to do.
focus: Explain the Batch Normalizing Transform (Algorithm 1) on a single activation over a small mini-batch. Let the learner edit the mini-batch values and the parameters gamma, beta and epsilon. Show the mini-batch mean, variance, normalized values and outputs. Check that normalized values have mean 0 and variance close to 1, and that gamma = sqrt(variance + eps), beta = mean recovers the original inputs. Explain the role of epsilon when all values are equal. Do not train a network.
audience: Second-year engineering undergraduate who knows mean and variance but not deep learning.
